scenarios.name: Choking
scenarios.description: When an object blocks the airway, preventing breathing.
steps: Ask the person 'Are you choking?' — if they cannot speak, cough, or breathe, act immediately.
Stand behind the person and wrap your arms around their waist.
Make a fist with one hand and place it just above the navel, below the ribcage.
Grasp your fist with the other hand and give 5 quick, upward abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver).
Repeat thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unconscious.
If unconscious: Lower them to the ground, call 911, and begin CPR.
doNot: Do NOT perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year — use back blows and chest thrusts instead
Do NOT try to blindly sweep the mouth with your finger
Do NOT give water to someone who is actively choking
scenarios.forInfants: For infants: 5 back blows (between shoulder blades) alternating with 5 chest thrusts (center of chest, just below nipple line).

scenarios.name: CPR (Cardiac Arrest)
scenarios.description: When someone's heart stops beating and they are unresponsive.
steps: Check for responsiveness — tap shoulders and shout 'Are you OK?'
Call 911 immediately (or have someone call). Get an AED if available.
Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
Push hard and fast — at least 2 inches deep, at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.
If trained: Give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions (30:2 ratio).
If not trained in rescue breaths: Continue hands-only CPR without stopping.
Use an AED as soon as available — follow its voice prompts.
Continue CPR until emergency services arrive or the person shows signs of life.
doNot: Do NOT stop compressions for more than 10 seconds
Do NOT be afraid of pushing too hard — broken ribs are better than death
Do NOT delay starting CPR to look for a pulse
scenarios.cprTiming: Push to the beat of 'Stayin' Alive' by the Bee Gees (100-120 BPM)

scenarios.name: Burns
scenarios.description: Tissue damage from heat, chemicals, electricity, or radiation.
steps: Remove the person from the source of the burn.
Cool the burn immediately with cool (not cold/ice) running water for at least 10-20 minutes.
Remove jewelry, watches, or tight clothing near the burn before swelling occurs.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-stick bandage or clean cloth.
Take over-the-counter pain relievers (ibuprofen or acetaminophen).
For minor burns: Apply aloe vera gel or burn cream after cooling.
doNot: Do NOT apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or home remedies to burns
Do NOT break blisters — they protect against infection
Do NOT remove clothing stuck to the burn
Do NOT use adhesive bandages directly on burns
scenarios.seekHelp: Seek emergency care for: burns larger than 3 inches, burns on face/hands/feet/genitals, chemical or electrical burns, burns that appear white or charred (3rd degree).

scenarios.name: Severe Bleeding
scenarios.description: Uncontrolled bleeding from a wound requiring immediate pressure.
steps: Call 911 for severe or uncontrolled bleeding.
Wear gloves if available to protect yourself.
Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound using a clean cloth or bandage.
Maintain constant pressure — do NOT lift the cloth to check the wound.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top without removing the first layer.
If possible, elevate the injured area above the level of the heart.
If bleeding doesn't stop with direct pressure, apply a tourniquet (if trained) 2-3 inches above the wound.
Note the time the tourniquet was applied and tell emergency responders.
doNot: Do NOT remove embedded objects from a wound — stabilize them in place
Do NOT apply a tourniquet unless direct pressure fails and the situation is life-threatening
Do NOT use a tourniquet on the neck or torso

scenarios.name: Fractures (Broken Bones)
scenarios.description: A break or crack in a bone, often from trauma or falls.
steps: Keep the person still — do NOT try to move or realign the broken bone.
Immobilize the injured area using a splint or sling (use rolled newspaper, cardboard, etc.).
Apply ice wrapped in a towel to reduce swelling — 20 minutes on, 20 off.
For open fractures (bone visible): Cover the wound with a sterile bandage, do NOT push bone back in.
Monitor for signs of shock: pale skin, rapid breathing, confusion.
Get to an emergency room or call 911 for severe fractures.
doNot: Do NOT try to straighten or push a bone back into place
Do NOT apply ice directly to skin
Do NOT let the person eat or drink (in case surgery is needed)
Do NOT move someone with a suspected spine or neck fracture

scenarios.name: Seizure
scenarios.description: Uncontrolled electrical disturbance in the brain causing convulsions.
steps: Stay calm and note the time the seizure starts.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects to prevent injury.
Gently guide the person to the ground if they are standing.
Place something soft under their head (folded jacket, pillow).
Turn them on their side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear.
Stay with the person until the seizure ends and they are fully conscious.
After the seizure: Speak calmly, help them sit up when ready.
doNot: Do NOT hold the person down or restrain their movements
Do NOT put anything in their mouth — they cannot swallow their tongue
Do NOT give food, water, or medication until fully alert
Do NOT leave them alone
scenarios.seekHelp: Call 911 if: seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, person doesn't regain consciousness, another seizure occurs, person is injured, or it's their first seizure.

scenarios.name: Severe Allergic Reaction (Anaphylaxis)
scenarios.description: Life-threatening allergic reaction causing airway swelling and shock.
steps: Call 911 immediately — anaphylaxis can be fatal within minutes.
If the person has an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen), help them use it in the outer thigh.
Have the person lie down with legs elevated (unless they have breathing difficulty — let them sit up).
Loosen tight clothing and cover them with a blanket.
If breathing stops, begin CPR.
A second dose of epinephrine can be given after 5-15 minutes if symptoms don't improve.
Even if symptoms improve after epinephrine, still go to the ER — reactions can return.
doNot: Do NOT give oral medication if the person is having trouble swallowing
Do NOT wait to see if symptoms improve before calling 911
Do NOT have the person stand or walk

scenarios.name: Heat Stroke
scenarios.description: Body temperature rises above 104°F (40°C) — a medical emergency.
steps: Call 911 immediately — heat stroke is life-threatening.
Move the person to a cool, shaded area or air-conditioned room.
Remove excess clothing.
Cool the person rapidly: apply ice packs to neck, armpits, and groin.
If possible, immerse in cool water or use a cool water spray with fanning.
Monitor body temperature and continue cooling until it drops below 101°F.
If conscious, give small sips of cool water.
doNot: Do NOT give aspirin or acetaminophen for heat stroke
Do NOT give fluids if the person is unconscious
Do NOT use ice-cold water immersion if elderly or has chronic illness

scenarios.name: Poisoning / Overdose
scenarios.description: Ingestion, inhalation, or exposure to a harmful substance.
steps: Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in US) or 911 immediately.
Try to identify the substance, amount, and time of exposure.
If the person is unconscious but breathing: place in recovery position.
If not breathing: begin CPR.
If poison is on the skin: remove contaminated clothing and rinse skin with water for 15-20 minutes.
If poison is in the eyes: rinse with clean water for 15-20 minutes.
Bring the container or substance to the hospital if possible.
doNot: Do NOT induce vomiting unless told to by Poison Control
Do NOT give activated charcoal without medical guidance
Do NOT give the person anything to eat or drink unless directed by Poison Control

scenarios.name: Nosebleed
scenarios.description: Bleeding from the nasal passages, usually from dry air or minor trauma.
steps: Sit upright and lean slightly forward (not backward).
Pinch the soft part of the nose (just below the bony bridge) firmly.
Hold the pinch for at least 10-15 minutes without releasing to check.
Breathe through the mouth while pinching.
Apply a cold compress or ice pack to the bridge of the nose.
After bleeding stops, avoid blowing nose, bending over, or heavy lifting for several hours.
doNot: Do NOT tilt the head backward — blood may flow into the throat
Do NOT stuff tissues or cotton deep into the nose
Do NOT pick or blow the nose after the bleeding stops
scenarios.seekHelp: See a doctor if: nosebleed lasts more than 20 minutes, follows a head injury, occurs frequently, or involves large amounts of blood.

scenarios.name: Sprains & Strains
scenarios.description: Stretched or torn ligaments (sprain) or muscles/tendons (strain).
steps: Follow R.I.C.E. protocol:
REST — Stop activity and avoid putting weight on the injured area.
ICE — Apply ice wrapped in a towel for 20 minutes every 2-3 hours for the first 48 hours.
COMPRESSION — Wrap the area with an elastic bandage (not too tight).
ELEVATION — Keep the injured area raised above heart level when possible.
Take over-the-counter pain relievers (ibuprofen) for pain and swelling.
After 48 hours, gentle range-of-motion exercises can begin.
doNot: Do NOT apply ice directly to skin
Do NOT wrap too tightly — check for numbness or tingling
Do NOT ignore severe pain or inability to bear weight (may be a fracture)
